title: The English Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Inglés
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The English Way is the short Camino. Six walking days take you from the old naval city of Ferrol, on Galicia's Atlantic coast, to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. It is ~113 km in all, which is small enough to hold in your head and big enough to change you a little.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this is your Camino, what each of the six days asks of you, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, and the chapter on the A Coruña start, which explains a choice many people puzzle over.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. Each day says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way". You can decide the rest later.
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service, and it does not pretend to be. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
Every distance here carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate. Published stage lengths differ from one source to the next, by up to about a kilometre, and this book says so where it matters. Where something depends on the season (a closure, a diversion, heat, a river after rain), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way. Each stamp is a
sello
. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules; you will meet those rules in plain language later in the book.
They are explained again when they first matter, and used plainly after that.
Pack lightly, walk gently, and take your time over the long hill.
Buen Camino.
Where it starts and ends

The Camino Inglés starts in Ferrol, a naval city on a long, sheltered inlet of the Atlantic, and ends at the cathedral in Santiago de Compostela. Every step is in Galicia, in the province of A Coruña. The official site of the association of councils along the route gives the length from Ferrol as ~113 km, and the Xunta de Galicia, the regional government, gives ~112 km. Other pages say ~110 km and ~119 km, and you will often see a rounded ~120 km. All of them describe the same road. This book uses ~113 km, which is also what the six stage figures add up to.
The usual six days, with the towns this book follows:

items.t: Day 1: Ferrol to Neda, ~15 km
Day 2: Neda to Pontedeume, ~13 km
Day 3: Pontedeume to Betanzos, ~20 km
Day 4: Betanzos to Hospital de Bruma, ~24 km
Day 5: Hospital de Bruma to Sigüeiro, ~24 km
Day 6: Sigüeiro to Santiago de Compostela, ~16 km

spans.t: Plans differ: the Xunta's stages and the official leaflet divide the route in other ways, and a later chapter shows how. These are the usual stage towns.
What it feels like

The first half belongs to the water. You leave Ferrol with the sea on your right for almost the whole of the first day, then follow the estuaries of the Eume and the Mandeo through small towns with arcaded streets, medieval bridges and Romanesque churches. The official site says the route starts at sea level and climbs inland without passing ~500 m, so this is a gentle Camino by the standards of the long ones.

Gentle does not mean flat. Several days begin with a steep climb, and the fourth day, over the hills between Betanzos and Hospital de Bruma, is the one the official site calls the most demanding. After that the path turns inland for good: woodland, hamlets, rural churches, a long gradual descent, a medieval bridge over the Tambre and, on the last morning, an oak forest called the Enchanted Forest before the city.
Why it exists

The Way of St James is a pilgrimage to the tomb of the apostle in Santiago. The Pilgrim's Office dates its beginning to the discovery of the tomb under King Alfonso II, who reigned from 792 to 842, and calls the twelfth and thirteenth centuries its golden age.

Most pilgrims walked or rode. Those from Britain, Ireland and northern Europe often took a ship instead, and landed on this coast. The official history says that for more than eight hundred years pilgrims came from northern Europe, mainly from Britain and Ireland, and that the sea route was especially popular from the thirteenth to the sixteenth centuries. A voyage took at least two to four weeks, wind and currents permitting. Ships sailed from at least thirty ports in the United Kingdom, with Bristol and Plymouth the busiest. A Coruña is named as the traditional landing port, and Ferrol, with its deep, sheltered harbour, is the start of the route today.

Some of the history is specific. The Xunta's route page records that in 1147 a troop of English, German and Flemish crusaders visited the tomb of St James. Wikipedia adds that during the Hundred Years' War, which ran from 1337 to 1453, English pilgrims and traders travelled to Galician ports with the permission of the English Crown. Among the travellers the official history page names is Margery Kempe, an English mystic who, according to Wikipedia, set off for Santiago in 1417. On the road itself, you will pass the remains of two medieval pilgrims' hospitals: one beside the clock tower in Neda, and the chapel of San Lourenzo at Hospital de Bruma, a village that still carries the memory of its hospital in its name. Wikipedia lists eight places where pilgrim hospitals had significant English support: Neda, Miño, Pontedeume, Betanzos, Bruma, Sigüeiro, San Paio and Paderne. In a real sense, the Camino Inglés is a string of old hospital towns.
Silence, and a revival

The Renaissance and the Reformation reduced the numbers of pilgrims on every route. For this one, the official site says it fell into oblivion in the eighteenth century and revived with great vitality in the 1990s. It is now a real Camino again. In 2024 about 26,800 pilgrims finished the English Way, the fourth most walked route to Santiago, according to the Pilgrim's Office statistics as reported by Wikipedia. That is quiet company compared with the busiest roads, but you will not be alone.

The name is English because of who came, not because the path is English. If you are walking from Britain, the association names Finchale Priory in County Durham as the official starting point of the Camino Inglés in England. From there you will need a ship, a plane or a great deal of patience to reach Ferrol.
How hard is it?

The official site rates four of the six days as low difficulty and two, the third and the fourth, as medium. It calls the fourth the most demanding, and the hardest for most pilgrims, while adding that this does not mean it is very difficult. The Xunta rates the whole route medium. In plain terms: nothing here needs mountaineering, and the highest ground stays under ~500 m. What it asks for is steady legs, good shoes and a willingness to walk in the rain.

The days are not long by Camino standards. The official planning page gives an average of ~20 to ~25 km a day and suggests five or six stages from Ferrol. This book uses six. The first two days are short, ~15 km and ~13 km, which is kind: you meet your feet before they meet the hills. The two longest days are the fourth and fifth, each ~24 km. The fourth is hilly, and the fifth is long but mostly downhill.
Who it suits

items.t: First-time pilgrims
who want to try a real Camino in about a week, without committing to a month.
Anyone with limited time
, such as a long weekend plus a few days, who still wants to arrive in Santiago on foot.
Walkers who want the Compostela
and meet the Pilgrim's Office rule of the last hundred kilometres. Ferrol is the one start on this route that reaches the full hundred (see the chapter on the A Coruña start).
Returners
who have walked the Francés or the Portugués and would like a quieter, shorter Way with a good deal of history.
People who like water and old towns.
The first three days run through estuary towns with medieval centres.
Those walking for a reason that needs quiet
: grief, a decision, a rest from work. Six days is a good length for it.

spans.t: Who might choose another

items.t: If you want a
long journey
, with weeks of walking and the rhythm of a long-distance life, choose a longer Camino. The Camino Francés is ~773 km, the Portugués Central ~240 km, the Norte ~820 km.
If you want the
sea beside you all the way
, the English Way gives you only the first half of that: the estuaries are in the first three days, and the rest is inland. The Portuguese Coastal Way, ~260 km, stays near the coast.
If you want
a big crowd
of fellow pilgrims every evening, this is not the busiest road. About one pilgrim in eighteen who arrived in Santiago in 2024 had walked it, by the Pilgrim's Office figure as reported by Wikipedia.
If you hope to earn the Compostela
from A Coruña alone
, it does not work: that start is ~74 km, short of the hundred. A later chapter explains the exceptions.
If you are a
cyclist
and want the Compostela, the rule is the last two hundred kilometres, and this route gives you ~113 km. You would need a longer approach by another route.

spans.t: Compared with its neighbours, in general terms

The English Way is about the same length as the last stretch of the Camino Francés from Sarria, which is ~115 km. It is a smaller company than the busiest roads, and its first half, along the estuaries, has a character of its own. On a quieter road there are fewer pilgrims to share news of a bed or a closed cafe, so plan each evening as carefully as each day. It is much shorter than the Portuguese and Northern Ways, and Ferrol and A Coruña both have train and bus stations, with Santiago's airport not far away.
Walking it alone

If you walk alone, know that the official site describes the route as passing through many populated areas, and still reminds you to keep your belongings in check. A few days on a quiet road is a good way to find out whether you like your own company. Tell someone your plan, and check in each evening. The chapter on body, weather and safety says more.
A short test

If you can walk ~20 km on a weekend, with a pack, in the shoes you plan to wear, and still want to walk the next day, you are ready. If you cannot yet, you have a month or two to train, and the chapter called "Before you go" tells you how.

The official site says the English Way can be walked at any time of the year. It also says that the thing to prepare for, in whichever season you choose, is rain. This chapter gives you patterns, not forecasts. For the weather on your own days, look at a forecast the evening before.
The shape of the year

Galicia has an Atlantic climate: mild, green and wet. The best long-term figures are for Santiago, at the end of the route. They describe a temperate oceanic climate with between ~1,500 and ~1,800 mm of rain a year, depending on which table you read. The wettest months are October, November, December and January. The driest and brightest are the summer months, and the official site says there is less rain on the route from May to September.

Temperatures stay moderate all year. In Santiago the average daily high in January is ~12 °C and the average low ~5 °C. In July the average high is ~25 °C and the low ~14 °C. Those are averages, so the days of a particular week can be warmer or colder, and a hot spell in summer is worth respecting.
Daylight

Daylight matters more than people expect. In Santiago it lasts ~9 hours around the shortest day in December and ~15 hours around the longest in June. Galicia sits at the western edge of Spain's time zone, so by the clock the sun comes up late and goes down late: close to nine o'clock on a midwinter morning, and a little after ten in the evening at midsummer.

For you that means two things. In winter, a ~24 km day has to fit into the light, and a late start can end in the dark. In summer you have the opposite luxury, and the sensible plan is to walk early, rest through the hottest hours, and enjoy the long evening.
How busy is it?
The Pilgrim's Office counts the pilgrims who finish each route. For the English Way in 2024, as reported by Wikipedia, the pattern by month was this:

items.t: January and February: ~130 and ~170 finishers
March: ~1,100
April: ~2,500
May, June and July: between ~3,200 and ~3,600 each
August: ~4,700, the busiest month
September: ~3,700
October: ~2,500
November and December: ~450 and ~320

spans.t: Read it as a rough guide. A month of ~2,500 is still dozens of pilgrims a day, so April and October are quiet without being empty. In August you will want to think about beds. In January the count works out at only a handful of pilgrims a day, so in the depth of winter you may walk for hours without meeting another one, and fewer places along the way may be open: another reason to check before you go.
What a season feels like

items.t: Spring
is a change from wet to drier. The days lengthen quickly, and the official site's drier season begins in May. Before that, expect showers and muddy paths: this is Galicia.
Summer
is the brightest and the busiest. Start early, carry water, and book ahead for the nights you cannot afford to be without a bed.
Autumn
trades the crowds of summer for the return of the rain. The light is still reasonable in October, and the walking is quiet.
Winter
is not cold by the figures above, but it is wet, with short days. It can be beautiful, and it asks for more planning, not less.

spans.t: Festivals and Holy Years

Towns on the way have their fiestas. Betanzos holds an August festival for San Roque with a very large paper balloon, and later in the month decorated boats go along the Mandeo to Os Caneiros, according to Wikipedia. Pontedeume's patron-saint festivities fall in September, on the 8th and 10th. A town in festival is wonderful and busy, so look at the dates when you plan your nights.
The next
Holy Year

, or Xacobeo, is 2027, then 2032. A Jacobean Holy Year falls whenever 25 July is a Sunday. The Holy Door of the cathedral is opened only in those years, and in a Holy Year the great censer, the botafumeiro, is used at all the Pilgrims' Masses. In the Holy Year of 2010 the Pilgrim's Office recorded 272,703 pilgrims who qualified for the Compostela, which gives you an idea of how many people the city welcomes. If you are walking in 2027, plan for a busier Santiago.
Check before you go

Closures, diversions, fires, storms and heat change from year to year. Before you set out, check the official Camino Inglés site and the current information in the CaminoPlus app for any change to the route or the services. If you are going in the quiet months, ask locally what is open.
The credencial
Your
credencial

is the pilgrim's passport. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago describes it as a card in a concertina fold, issued by a confraternity or an authorised association, by a parish church, or by a pilgrim hostel, and available both in Spain and abroad. It does two practical things: it opens the doors of the pilgrim hostels, and it is your proof when you ask for the Compostela. The Office is plain about it: the credencial "does not generate any rights", so it is a document of welcome, not a ticket.

If you can, get it before you leave home from a confraternity or association in your own country. If not, the official English Way site says that in Ferrol it is available at the co-cathedral of San Julián, known locally as San Xiao. Opening hours change with the season, so do not count on a visit on your first evening: check ahead.
You fill it with
sellos

, the stamps. The Office says they are normally collected where you sleep, but also in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. Ask for each one to show the date, the place and the seal of whoever stamps it. The official site recommends at least two stamps a day over the last hundred kilometres, which on this route means almost every day of the walk. If you walk only the minimum distance for the Compostela, the Office asks for a stamp at the start and the end of each stage, with the date.

The Pilgrim's Office also mentions a digital credential, developed as an app. If you plan to rely on one, ask the Office first. Until you have heard otherwise, carry the paper credencial in a plastic sleeve, and treat the stamps in any other app as a keepsake.
Getting there and back

Most pilgrims fly. Santiago airport (SCQ) is ~12 km from the city, with a city bus into town, and it has flights from Spanish cities and from London, Dublin, Paris, Frankfurt and others. A Coruña has its own airport (LCG), and the official site lists that one first for Ferrol, with Santiago second.

Ferrol has a train station and a bus station, and so does A Coruña. From an airport you will need a bus or a train to reach Ferrol, and the connections are not always direct. Timetables change, so look them up a few days before you travel. Give yourself a night in Ferrol before you start: it is a good way to find your credencial, eat properly and check your pack.

Going home is easier, because you will be in a city with an airport, a train station and a bus station. Do not book a flight for the morning after you arrive. A day or two in Santiago is not a luxury, as the chapter on arriving explains.
Training
Six days is gentle, and you do not need to be an athlete, but your feet and legs need to know what is coming. Two months is plenty.

items.t: Walk most days, a few kilometres at first, with the shoes and socks you will wear.
Add a longer walk each weekend, building towards ~20 km with your loaded pack. Try to do one of them in the rain.
Include hills or stairs. The fourth day starts with a climb, and the third day's first kilometre out of Pontedeume is steep.
Walk two days in a row at least once. The second day is the one that teaches you.

spans.t: If you have a health condition, or have not been active for a long time, talk to your doctor before you begin.
Packing
Carry as little as you can. Everything you pack, you will lift every morning.

items.t: A rain jacket or poncho, and a cover for your pack. The official site says the thing to prepare for is rain.
Quick-drying clothes in layers, rather than cotton, and a hat for sun and for rain.
A light sleeping bag or a liner for the hostels, a small quick-drying towel, and sandals for the evenings.
Earplugs and a head torch, which help in a dormitory and on a dark morning.
A water bottle, a small first-aid kit with blister dressings, and any medicines you take.
Your phone, charger and a plug adapter, and a copy of your passport or identity card.
Your credencial, in a plastic sleeve.

spans.t: Download your map before you leave home, because signal is not guaranteed on a forest track.
Shoes and feet

Your feet are the whole journey. Wear shoes that are well broken in, and not new, with room for the toes to swell a little over the day. Choose socks that wick moisture, and carry a spare pair. At the first sign of a hot spot, stop and deal with it, dressing it before it becomes a blister. Take off your shoes and let your feet air at lunch.
A short first day is a gift. Use it to find out what your feet think of the day.
Money in general terms

Spain uses the euro. Carry a bank card, and some cash in small notes for the small places that do not take cards. Withdraw cash in the larger towns, before a stretch of hamlets, and not in the last village before a long day. The book gives no prices because they change; ask what things cost before you commit, and use the app for stays.
Language

Galicia has two official languages, Galician and Spanish. You will see both on signs, and the official site is available in both and in English. Spanish will get you through, and a few words of it go a long way:
buenos días
gracias
por favor
¿tiene una cama?
Galician names look unfamiliar at first: the article is
A
or
O
("the"), as in A Sionlla and O Hospital, and a place can be spelt Xuvia or Xubia on different maps. They are the same village.
Most people you meet in a small place will be glad of a greeting. Say it first.

chapters.title: The ría days: Ferrol to Betanzos

spans.t: The character of these days
The first three days belong to the water. You walk out of a naval city with an inlet of the Atlantic on your right, a
ría

, as Galicians call these long sea inlets, and you follow the estuaries of the Eume, the Lambre and the Mandeo through small towns that grew up where the tide ends. The days are short at first (~15 km, ~13 km) and then longer (~20 km). Every night is in a town with an old centre, and the second and third days each bring you to an old bridge.

The distances in this book come from the official English Way site. The Xunta de Galicia and the federation of friends of the Camino give slightly different figures, by up to about a kilometre, and the official site's own pages disagree with each other in one place. Treat every figure as a good guide, not as a measurement.
Day 1: Ferrol to Neda (~15 km)

The official site rates this day low, and estimates three to four hours. It is the gentlest start on offer, and an unusual one: you leave a naval city by its harbour. Ferrol has built ships for most of its history, the Royal Dockyards were built between 1726 and 1783, and its sheltered harbour is often called the best natural port in Europe. The official route starts at the port of Curuxeiras, in the old quarter, and crosses the city by the Calle Real, with the naval-military area on your right. Take a moment for the co-cathedral of San Xiao and the convent of San Francisco before the town falls away.

Then the sea takes over. It stays on your right for almost the whole day. Ferrol and Neda are only ~7 km apart as a gull flies, but the path has to go right round the head of the inlet, which is why a short line becomes a ~15 km walk. Along the way you pass the Romanesque monastery of San Martiño de Xuvia, once a double monastery, with three Romanesque apses and a medieval sarcophagus in its atrium, in front of an eighteenth-century tower. Shortly after leaving Narón you pass the Royal Flour Factory, built in 1775 and now a visitor centre. The official gastronomy page lists the bread of Neda, and a visit to the town's wheat mills.

In Neda you will find the churches of Santa María and the Gothic San Nicolás. The official site says you can stop here or go on ~16 km to Pontedeume. This book stops, because a short first day is not a weakness. Get your first
sello
before you leave Ferrol and a second here. Then wash your socks, look at your feet, and eat something local.
Day 2: Neda to Pontedeume (~13 km)
The official site rates this day low and calls it a quiet stage with only one climb, at the exit of Neda. It is the shortest day of the walk, and the one where the Camino is closest to a stroll.

Leaving Neda, you pass the churches again, cross the River Belelle by a footbridge, and join the old arcaded Calle Real. In the middle of it stand the Clock Tower and the Town Hall, beside the remains of the old pilgrims' hospital, dedicated to the Holy Spirit. It is the first of the hospitals that this road remembers, and it is worth stopping for. At San Nicolás the official site points out one of the oldest crosses in Galicia.

The climb out of the town is the only real one of the day, and from the top you can see the Ferrol ría, which shows you how far you have already come. After a washing place and a fountain you pass Fene, a town with services for pilgrims. Beyond the washing place of Mundín, a dirt track climbs towards the town hall of Cabanas. As you drop into Cabanas you see the mouth of the River Eume. A few kilometres upstream it forms the Fragas do Eume Natural Park. Ahead, on the mountain, you can see the castle of Nogueirosa, which Wikipedia credits to Fernán Pérez de Andrade, the fourteenth-century knight known as
o Bóo
, "the good one".

The bridge over the Eume used to be far longer. The official site says it has only 15 arches today and once had 70. On the far side, Pontedeume is a town founded by a charter of Alfonso X the Wise in 1270, with arcades, wooden balconies and glass galleries. The historic quarter holds the Tower of Andrade, part of the palace of the Andrade family, the church of Santiago, the Town Hall and the Augustinian convent.

The official site's two pages disagree about this stage: one says ~13 km from Neda to Pontedeume, another says ~16 km. Expect ~13. Do not push on. Tomorrow starts with a steep kilometre, and the best use of this afternoon is to rest.
Day 3: Pontedeume to Betanzos (~20 km)

This is the first medium day, with an estimate of about six hours. The official site gives the one warning that matters: the exit from Pontedeume is a steep slope of one kilometre. After that the climbing eases into a gentle descent through farmland, down to sea level at the Baxoi bridge, which the official site says pilgrims crossed in the Middle Ages. From here the tide is close again.

The path passes Miño and enters the mouth of the Lambre, part of the Natura 2000 network of protected areas, where you follow the river for a short stretch and cross a Gothic bridge. Then you climb to a viewpoint above the mouth of the Mandeo, the estuary of Betanzos. The descent goes through vineyards to the Romanesque church of San Martiño de Tiobre, which the official site calls an obligatory stop. The wine of these vineyards was once famous, and the site says it was sought after by the British Navy: a small reminder of how many ties this coast had with Britain.

One more climb brings you to Os Remedios, a Renaissance church, which the official site calls something rare in Galicia. Then you cross the old bridge over the Mandeo and enter Betanzos by the gate of A Ponte Vella.

Betanzos has one of the best preserved old quarters in Galicia, and it is worth an evening. The church of San Francisco was built in 1387 by order of Fernán Pérez de Andrade, and his tomb, carved with hunting scenes, is inside. The church of Santiago, from the fifteenth century, was built by the tailors' guild, and has a portal with an equestrian statue of the saint. The town's omelette, the
tortilla de Betanzos
, is a local speciality.

The Xunta's own stages end at Miño, and the official leaflet splits this day there too, into two walks of ~10 km each. If your feet are tired after the climbs, that is a fair plan. Whichever you choose, it is the longest day so far, so carry lunch.

chapters.title: Over the hills: Betanzos to Santiago

spans.t: The character of these days

After Betanzos the Camino turns its back on the sea and goes inland for good. The next three days are woodland, hamlets, small rural churches and a long, gradual descent into the valley of the Tambre. There are fewer towns and more country, so the evenings need as much planning as the days. The two branches of the Way, the one from Ferrol and the one from A Coruña, become one, and the last two days are shared by everyone who walks to Santiago this way.
Day 4: Betanzos to Hospital de Bruma (~24 km)

The official site calls this the most demanding stage, and the hardest for most pilgrims, and in the same breath adds that this does not mean it is very difficult. It rates it medium and estimates about eight hours. The climbing starts almost as soon as you leave Betanzos, and it is the one day on this Camino that asks you to be patient with yourself.

You leave Betanzos by the bridge of As Cascas, which the official site says survived the war against Napoleon's soldiers. Then you climb the first hill, and the day goes on through hills and forest. Three rural churches mark the way: Cos, with its church of San Esteban; the sanctuary of Nosa Señora da Saleta at Presedo, which vegetation hides, ~100 m from the path; and Leiro. Nowhere does the Camino rise above ~500 m, the official site says, but this is the day when you will feel that you are climbing.

At the chapel of As Travesas, where there are tables and benches, the branch from A Coruña joins the Way. This is the place to sit down. After it you have just over ~2 km to Hospital de Bruma, and for part of that you walk beside the main road. The official site advises caution there. Where you must walk on a road, face the traffic, keep well to the edge, and do not let tiredness make you careless.
Hospital de Bruma, in the municipality of Mesía, keeps the chapel of San Lourenzo, the remains of a medieval pilgrims' hospital. The village's name remembers what stood here.

You can divide this day. The official leaflet splits it at Presedo, into ~12 km and ~11.5 km. Start early, eat before the long climb, and carry food and water for the day, since the path passes through woodland and small hamlets, not through towns. On this day, the pace of the slowest hill is the right pace.
Day 5: Hospital de Bruma to Sigüeiro (~24 km)

After the hills, a gift. The official site rates this day low and describes it as a gradual descent from Bruma to Sigüeiro, the opposite of the day before. It estimates about six hours, but it is long, and a long downhill is hard on knees as well as being kind to lungs. Shorten your stride, and use your poles, if you carry them, on the steep places.

In the first two hours the path passes three churches: Ardemil, San Paio de Buscás and Calle. The official site recommends stopping at San Paio, which has a Romanesque façade and a polychrome figure of the saint. Then the way runs mostly through woodland. The site singles out a trail that starts in the village of Os Carrás, which keeps much of its medieval look.

About an hour before Sigüeiro you come to the Fonte da Santiña, a water point. The official site links it to Father Sarmiento, who stopped there in the eighteenth century. It is a useful place to refill your bottle. Then a medieval path takes you into the Carboeiro park and down to the River Tambre and its historic bridge at Sigüeiro. The day crosses the municipalities of Mesía, Ordes and Oroso.

The official leaflet splits this stage at Poulo, into ~10 km and ~15 km. It is the day where a plan helps most, because you will want to know before you start where you will sleep. The chapter on other ways to split the days says what the official site lists, and the CaminoPlus app is the place for the live answer.
Day 6: Sigüeiro to Santiago de Compostela (~16 km)

The last day is rated low and estimated at about four and a half hours. It begins well. The day opens with the crossing of the Tambre bridge, which the official site says has stood in the same place for almost a thousand years. Take the stairs on the left if you want a better view of it.

Then small tracks with little traffic run parallel to the right-hand side of the N-550, a main road. You will hear it more than you use it. Keep to the tracks. Pine woods lead to A Sionlla, where the ground turns to earth and the path goes round a prehistoric castro, the fortified settlement of a people who lived here long before any pilgrim. Then comes an oak wood called the Enchanted Forest, and the path drops towards farmland.
Shortly after the farmland, the route enters the centre of Santiago and heads for the cathedral.

Do not be surprised if you feel less than you expected, or more. There is no need to hurry the last streets. The cathedral has waited for pilgrims for centuries, and the chapter on arriving tells you what to do when you get there: where to go for the Compostela, what to expect, and how to give the next day a gentle shape.

chapters.title: The A Coruña start, and other ways to split the days

spans.t: The hundred-kilometre rule, in plain words

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons and meet its rules. On foot or on horseback, the Office asks for the last hundred kilometres on a single recognised route, in one continuous stretch, with the last stage ending at the cathedral. By bicycle it asks for the last two hundred. Your stamped credencial is the proof.

The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

The English Way is only just long enough to meet the rule. From Ferrol it is ~113 km, so you can start there and qualify. Add up the stage figures in this book and you will see how little margin there is: from Neda, the next stage town, you would have ~98 km left, which falls just short. That is why many pilgrims start in Ferrol. Wikipedia says that Ferrol is the only start on this route in Spain that is far enough from Santiago, and the official English Way site calls Ferrol a perfectly valid starting point for the Compostela.

If you start in Ferrol, walk every stage on foot and keep your credencial stamped, you meet the distance and the stamp rules, and the Office will talk to you about the rest when you arrive. A word of caution on the figures: published lengths differ by a kilometre or two, and one page of the official site gives ~119 km for the whole route. If you are planning a start close to the limit, ask the Office.
Starting in A Coruña

The Camino Inglés has a second start in A Coruña, the city of the Tower of Hercules. This is a shorter variant: the official English Way site gives it as ~74 km, the Xunta as ~73 km. The official site calls it the Camiño do Faro, the Lighthouse Way, after the Roman lighthouse that still stands in the city. A Coruña is the traditional landing port of the sea pilgrims, and the official history names it as the great meeting point of those who came by ship.

It can be walked in three or four days. The official stages are A Coruña to Sergude (~20 km), Sergude to Bruma (~13 km), and then the two stages shared with the Ferrol branch. The two branches meet at the chapel of As Travesas, just over ~2 km before Hospital de Bruma. The official site calls the second stage physically very demanding because of its long climb, and very rewarding for the landscape. You can also walk from A Coruña to Bruma in one day, which the site puts at ~33 km.

Fewer pilgrims choose it. In 2024, as Wikipedia reports from the Pilgrim's Office statistics, about 96 per cent of those who finished the English Way started in Ferrol and about 2 per cent in A Coruña.
Why A Coruña alone does not give the Compostela

At ~74 km, the A Coruña route is short of a hundred. The Office's rules do contain a provision for people who have already walked a recognised route outside Spain: they need no less than seventy kilometres in Spain. The A Coruña route is a little more than that. The Office also says the Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special cases, and that it should be contacted in advance.

The official English Way site describes a way to make up the distance with an earlier walk, and Wikipedia reports a rule from December 2016 which it states as a certified twenty-five kilometres on a pilgrimage route linked to St James in the walker's own country. The sources describe the rule differently, and rules change. For that reason this book does not tell you it works. If you want the Compostela and plan to start in A Coruña, ask the Pilgrim's Office, before you go, what it accepts in your case. The official site also says that segments of different Caminos cannot be mixed, so ask about yours.

In England, the association names Finchale Priory in County Durham as the official English starting point, and a route there was recognised in 2019. Whether a walk on that route counts towards the Compostela is for the Pilgrim's Office to say.
Other ways to split the six days
The six stages in this book are the usual stage towns. They are not the only plan.

items.t: Five days.

The official planning page says five or six stages from Ferrol. The Xunta's own stages are Ferrol to Neda, Neda to Miño (~22 km), Miño to Bruma (~35 km), Bruma to Sigüeiro and Sigüeiro to Santiago. A ~35 km day is a long one for most people, and this book does not suggest it.
Seven, eight or nine days.

The official leaflet divides the long days into shorter sections: Pontedeume to Miño (~10 km) and Miño to Betanzos (~10 km); Betanzos to Presedo (~12 km) and Presedo to Bruma (~11.5 km); and Bruma to Poulo (~10 km) and Poulo to Sigüeiro (~15 km). Add one split and you have seven days; add all three and you have nine.
A slow plan.
If you have time, take any of these and add a rest day at Betanzos. It is a town worth an afternoon.

spans.t: Where you will sleep

Which towns have a public hostel, and which are open this month, changes from season to season, so this book does not list them. Use the CaminoPlus app and the official English Way site for where to sleep tonight, and ask locally for tomorrow. How the hostels work is in the chapter on sleeping, eating and resting. The official site also lists baggage-transport services if you would rather walk with a lighter pack; ask which cover your days.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office lists access to "hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way" as the first practical use of the credencial, and notes that hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

On this Camino the official site says public hostels generally work on a first come, first served basis and generally for one night. Private hostels, hotels and guesthouses can be booked ahead. Dogs are allowed on the route, but public hostels generally do not let them sleep inside, so ask before you arrive with one. Details change from year to year, and a call or a message ahead saves a tired evening.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and do not rustle bags at night or before dawn. Pack your rucksack in the hall.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed. Shoes belong where the house puts them.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. Somebody will snore, and if it is you, apologise at breakfast.
Keep your valuables close, as the official site advises for belongings generally.

spans.t: Bedbugs

are a risk in any shared bed anywhere. Check the seams of the mattress, keep your pack and clothes off the bed, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is not a reason to avoid hostels, only a reason to look before you lie down.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating. A good night is part of the walk.
Eating
Many places along the Way offer a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what is on it and what it costs before you sit. A set meal is a good way to eat well on a long day, and it is an easy way to try what the region cooks.
The official site's gastronomy page is a short guide to what to look for as you go. It names the
tortilla de Betanzos

, the omelette of the town, and the cabbage of Betanzos. It names the bread of Neda, and the baked specialities of Pontedeume: proia, costrada, melindres and almendrados. In the country between Betanzos and Santiago it lists trout from Oroso, and the cheeses of Abegondo, Paderne, Mesía and Ordes, some of which carry the Arzúa-Ulloa denomination. It also names dishes that belong to the whole route:
polbo á feira
, the Galician octopus, empanadas, honey and the
tarta de Santiago
, the almond cake. Near the coast it points to fish and seafood. Galician wines and
queimada
complete the list.
You do not need to eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day, and eat it without a screen.

Water matters as much. Fill your bottle in each town, because some stretches pass only through woods and hamlets, and take food for the long days, the fourth and the fifth. The Fonte da Santiña, an hour before Sigüeiro, is a named water point on the fifth day.
Resting
The English Way is short, and it is easy to treat it as a sprint. Resist that. A day of rest is part of the walk.

If you have a day to spare, spend it in Betanzos, which has one of the best preserved old quarters in Galicia, with two great medieval churches, an old bridge and a medieval gate. It comes at the end of the third day, and the fourth, the next, is the hardest of the walk. If you can only rest once on the way, rest there.
The other good place is the end. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it deserves more than a night. The chapter on arriving says why.

On the road, listen to your body before you listen to your plan. Take the short days as short days. If something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.

This chapter is plain on purpose. Nothing here is a reason to be afraid of the English Way, which the official site rates low to medium and which stays under ~500 m. It is a list of the things worth taking seriously.
Feet and legs

Your feet decide how the walk goes. Stop at the first hot spot and dress it, before it becomes a blister. Change your socks at lunch if they are damp. Rest for a few minutes each hour, take your pack off, and eat and drink before you are hungry or thirsty. If you feel a sharp or growing pain in a knee, a shin or the top of a foot, stop. Rest it for a day, or take a shorter stage. A day lost to rest is better than a week lost to an injury.
Rain and cold

Rain is the thing to prepare for, as the official site says. Wet clothes cool you quickly, even in mild weather. Carry a waterproof jacket and a pack cover, and keep one dry layer in a bag that cannot get wet. Paths, steps and old stones are slippery in the wet, so shorten your stride and use your poles, if you have them.

In Santiago the average daily high in January is ~12 °C and the low ~5 °C, and the daylight lasts only ~9 hours at the shortest. In cold, wet weather, if you start to shiver, stop in a warm place before you try to go on. Do not start a long day in the dark.
Heat

July averages in Santiago are ~25 °C by day, and a hot spell can be far warmer than the average. On a hot day, start early, wear a hat, put on sun cream, and carry more water than you think you need. Rest in the shade through the hottest hours. A headache, dizziness or nausea in the heat are signs to stop, get into the shade, and drink. If they do not pass, ask for help.
Roads, paths and dogs

Most of the way is on tracks and paths. The official site says the Camino Inglés is clearly signposted along most of its route, with yellow arrows on milestones and at key points, and it suggests a map for the hidden details. Two stretches are close to traffic. On the fourth day, just before Hospital de Bruma, the path runs beside the main road, and the official site advises caution. On the sixth day the path runs parallel to the N-550 on small tracks with little traffic, and you should stay on the tracks.
Wherever you must walk on a road, face the oncoming traffic, keep well to the edge, and wear something bright. Never walk on a road in the dark.
Dogs on farms may bark as you pass. Walk on calmly and do not stare or run. If you are afraid of them, ask in the village before you set out.
Staying safe on your own

The official site notes that the route passes through many populated areas, and also reminds you to keep your belongings in check. Tell someone where you plan to sleep each night, and message them when you arrive. Keep your phone charged, carry your map offline, and know the name of the last village you passed.
When to stop

Stop, and get help, for chest pain, a fever, severe dizziness, a fall with a blow to the head, a swollen joint, or anything that frightens you. A doctor is the right person for a worry, and a plan can always change. The Way will still be there.
Emergencies
is the European emergency number and it works in Spain. Say where you are as exactly as you can: the village, the stage and the last landmark you passed.
Check before you go

In dry summers, ask locally about fires and any closed paths. After heavy rain, ask about flooded sections and slippery descents. Closures and diversions change, so look at the official site and the current information in the app before each day.

People walk to Santiago for many reasons, and they do not have to be the same as yours. Some walk out of faith: the Way is a Christian pilgrimage to the tomb of the apostle James, and the Pilgrim's Office gives the Compostela to those who come for religious or spiritual reasons. Some walk for sport, or for a rest from work, or because a friend did. Some walk out of grief, or at a turning point, when a life needs a pause. Some walk simply because they are curious about what six days of walking will do. All of these are welcome on the road, and none of them needs defending.
What the road does

A short Camino has its own gift. Six days is long enough to leave your phone in your pocket for an hour, then for an afternoon, and short enough that you can take the time off without a great arrangement. On the English Way the first days run beside water, and water has a way of slowing the mind. Then the road climbs, and the hills teach patience. Then it goes through woods, and the woods teach attention. By the last morning, in the oak forest before the city, many walkers find they have stopped counting kilometres.

There is also an old story under your feet. For centuries people came here by sea, after weeks on a ship, to set foot on this coast and walk the last stretch on land. The official site says the voyage took at least two to four weeks, wind and currents permitting. Think of them when you cross the old bridge at Pontedeume or sit in the shade of a church. They did not have a map on a phone, and you are not the first to be tired here.
Walking with a question
You do not need a question, but if you have one, it will keep you company. Here are a few for the days, one for each stage, to take or leave.

items.t: Ferrol to Neda.
What did you bring that you do not need? You can put some of it down.
Neda to Pontedeume.
Whom are you walking with, even if you walk alone?
Pontedeume to Betanzos.
What is a hill you have climbed before, and what did it take?
Betanzos to Hospital de Bruma.
What is the hard thing in front of you, and what is the next small step?
Hospital de Bruma to Sigüeiro.
What can you let go of, as the road lets go of the hills?
Sigüeiro to Santiago.
What do you hope to carry home, and what will you leave here?

spans.t: For every kind of walker

If you walk with faith, you will find churches along the way, open some of the time, where you can sit quietly or pray. If you do not, you will find the same places quiet and cool, and worth a rest. If your reason is grief, give yourself permission to cry on the road: most walkers will understand. If you walk to get fit, let the beauty in anyway. The road itself does not ask you for a reason at the door. It only asks you to keep walking.
The cathedral

The Camino Inglés ends where every Way ends: at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, built over the reputed tomb of St James. Wikipedia dates the start of construction to 1075 and the consecration to 1211. It is a Romanesque building with Gothic and Baroque additions. The Pórtico da Gloria, the carved Romanesque doorway inside, was completed by Master Mateo in 1188, and the great Baroque façade on the Praza do Obradoiro, the square in front of it, was finished in 1740. The old town around it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.

The cathedral keeps a Holy Door, opened only in a Jacobean Holy Year, and the next Holy Year is 2027. Also kept there is the botafumeiro, the great censer, which Wikipedia says is swung on certain important religious days, and at all the Pilgrims' Masses in Holy Years.
Take a moment in the square before you do anything else. Sit on the stones if you wish. Many people find that the arrival is quieter or noisier than they expected.
The Pilgrim's Office and the Compostela
The
Compostela

is the certificate of your pilgrimage, written in Latin, and the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues it. The Office says that it is for those who have come to the tomb for religious or spiritual reasons, on foot, by bicycle or on horseback, and who have travelled at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred by bicycle. The Latin text speaks of those who come
devotionis affectu, voti vel pietatis
, which the Office's own English translation renders as coming "with an attitude of devotion or because of a vow or promise". The Office issues it without charge.

What to bring is simple: your credencial, stamped along the way, with the date, the place and the seal in each box. You also take a ticket with a QR code, which lets you follow your place in the queue on your phone. The Office warns that in times of great influx it cannot guarantee that you will receive the Compostela on the same day. In August, or in a Holy Year, arrive with that in mind. The Office's own website gives its address and its current hours, which are not in this book because they change.
If you walked for other reasons, or are not sure that your reasons count, the Office also offers a separate
certificate of distance
. It records where you began, how many kilometres you walked, the dates and the route, whatever your starting point. It carries a fee, and the Office gives the amount.
The Office meets a great many people in a day. Be patient, be warm, and if you have a doubt about your credencial, ask before you queue.
The pilgrims' Mass

The cathedral holds a Pilgrims' Mass. Check the cathedral's own website for the time, which changes. You do not need to be a believer to sit at the back and listen. It is a cathedral full of people who have walked.
The next day

Try not to leave on the morning after you arrive. A day in Santiago lets the walk settle. Wash your clothes, sleep late, and look at the old town. You may like to see the Hostal dos Reis Católicos, which the Catholic Monarchs founded in the sixteenth century as the Royal Hospital for pilgrims, and which has been a hotel since 1954, according to the Pilgrim's Office.

If you still have legs and time, some pilgrims walk on to Finisterre and Muxía on the coast, ~90 km farther, a route you will find in the CaminoPlus app's list. If you do not, buy a postcard and write to someone you walked with in your head.

The walk ends on a Tuesday afternoon, or a Saturday, or whenever it ends, and then you are back in a kitchen with a washing machine and a phone full of messages. You may find the first days at home odd. The pace is faster, the rooms are louder, and the thing you carried for six days has no obvious place to go.
Be gentle with yourself. A few small habits help.

items.t: Keep your credencial.
The stamps are a record of where you slept, and the pages will mean more in ten years than they do now. Put it where you will see it.
Write it down.
Three lines a day for the first week, about a place, a person or a feeling, are enough. The details go fast.
Keep one thing from the road.
An early walk before work, a minute of silence at lunch, a Sunday spent on foot. One habit is enough.
Tell someone.
The people who did not walk with you will want a story. Give them one, and keep one back for yourself.
Mend your feet, and thank them.

spans.t: The Way has a habit of calling people back. Some walk the Camino Inglés once and know it was enough. Others find themselves looking at a map of the Portuguese or the French Way a month later. If that is you, you have time. Rest, then plan, and be ready to carry less next time.
Buen Camino
, whenever you set out again.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus
. The app is still in development, so look in the app for what is available on the English Way today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.
A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in any app is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and the fact ledger that goes with it lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Asociación de Concellos do Camiño Inglés

, the official English Way site (caminoingles.gal): the stage figures and descriptions, the history page, the planning page, the questions and answers, the gastronomy page, the transport page and the A Coruña route.
The Xunta de Galicia
, the regional government, on its official Camino de Santiago portal (caminodesantiago.gal): the length of the route, its stages and the Neda to Miño stage.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the rules of the Compostela, the credencial, the certificate of distance and the history of the pilgrimage.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): the rule for the Compostela, the credencial and the certificate.
Wikipedia

, for history and geography: the articles on the English Way, Ferrol, Pontedeume, Betanzos, Santiago de Compostela and its cathedral, A Coruña, Galicia, Spain, the Jacobean Holy Year, Margery Kempe, Fernán Pérez de Andrade and Santiago airport. It is also where this book found the Pilgrim's Office statistics for 2024.
Published day-length tables for Santiago de Compostela
, checked against a standard solar calculation, for the hours of daylight in December and June.
The CaminoPlus route catalog

, for the names and order of the six stages. Stage lengths were compared with the Xunta portal and with a dossier on the Camino Inglés by the Spanish federation of associations of friends of the Camino, published in April 2024.

spans.t: Published stage lengths differ by up to about a kilometre, and a few pages disagree with themselves, so every distance in this book is marked ~. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the towns and villages who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Castro
: a prehistoric fortified settlement.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Ría
: a long sea inlet, as at Ferrol and Betanzos.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Xacobeo
: the Galician name for a Holy Year.
